 Michigan Secretary of State mobile office brings services directly to Detroit students and families
 Since 2021, the Michigan Secretary of State Mobile Office partnership brings Michigan Secretary of State services directly to DPSCD high schools, helping students and families access IDs, voter registration and other essential services.
 By Newsroom 
 ● 
 Building Communities 
 ● 
 November 18, 2026 
 The Michigan Secretary of State Mobile Office delivers convenience and government service accessibility to Detroit Public Schools Community District (DPSCD) students and their families through community engagement and inclusivity.
 The initiative began in 2021 with the Government Community Affairs Department’s desire to support DPSCD students and their families while simultaneously making Secretary of State services more accessible. When the opportunity arose, Orion Watson, a program associate with the department, jumped at the opportunity.
 “At that time, the Secretary of State, Jocelyn Benson, was putting more resources into the mobile unit program, and they wanted to engage more underserved communities that did not have the opportunity or resources to access the Secretary of State’s services. When we heard about her intentions, we reached out to develop that partnership,” said Watson. “Since then, we’ve had a yearly partnership where the Secretary of State Mobile Unit Team schedules to go to every DPSCD high school to provide their services for not only the students but for staff and families, to be able to access all of the services they offer at the branch offices — with the exception of a road test.”
 The Michigan Secretary of State Mobile Office visits Detroit Public Schools Community District high schools to provide services including first-time state IDs, driver’s license renewals, vehicle transactions, voter registration and REAL ID upgrades. DPSCD 
 Since its inception, the MSOSMO-DPSCD partnership has provided first-time IDs, driver’s license renewals, vehicle transactions, voter registration, and REAL ID upgrades on site at DPSCD high schools. In 2024 alone, MSOSMO visited 22 DPSCD high schools and equipped 670 students with State IDs while providing 149 community members and 74 staff members with additional services that same year. 
 Student ID requirements are essential for many extracurricular activities, and mandatory for summer employment programs; however, existing barriers hinder some students from securing these documents. Watson notes that lack of internet access, technology illiteracy, appointment restrictions, mobility issues and financial limitations are common barriers to state ID registration. 
 “With the new process of going to the Secretary of State, you have to have internet access, be able to make an appointment, and then  wait until that appointment is available, or go to some other [often] far away location. They don’t accept walk-ins anymore.” said Watson. “This is a way of making sure that our DPSCD students and our families that may not be as tech savvy,  have internet access, or may not have the ability to wait the process out to be able to access all of the services needed from the Secretary of State.”
 DPSCD students and families can access Secretary of State services at their schools, reducing barriers such as transportation, internet access and appointment availability. DPSCD 
 Thanks to a fiscal sponsorship in part by the Detroit Change Initiative, all DPSCD students are eligible for their state IDs free of cost. By waiving state ID registration fees and delivering SOS services to families and community members directly, MSOSMO meets underserved communities where they are without bias or restriction. The program accepts all forms of payment and offers hands-on guidance like application assistance for parents and younger siblings seeking to obtain their Michigan state issued ID.
 The program also serves a dual purpose: encouraging civic duty and building confidence while teaching teens life skills for independence. Students ages 16 and 17 who register for a state ID are automatically preregistered to vote, and they receive a voter registration card by mail once they reach voting age. This year, 184 students were taken to the polls as first-time voters as part of the 2026 “Get out to vote” campaign.
 The mobile office provides hands-on assistance with state ID applications, voter registration and other Secretary of State services for students, staff and families. DPSCD 
 “The students were really excited to be first-time voters, and we’re just glad to have the opportunity for their voices to be heard,” said Watson, who is especially proud of the program’s impact on students, families and communities across the city. The life skills students learn outside the classroom, such as civic engagement, activism and community development, he says, can last a lifetime. Mobilizing services has also created new access in Southwest Detroit, where recent immigration laws have threatened residents’ morale and safety. Participating residents are no longer fearful of deportation or other immigration concerns simply for accessing government services.
 Despite the program’s reach over the years, Watson would be remiss not to acknowledge the shared team effort behind the scenes.
 “It’s way bigger than me. It’s not just myself that does this work.” Watson said. ”[There’s] my coworker Dr. Carol Weaver, my partner in crime and then we have the person over the district – [DPSCD Executive director of Political and community engagement], Tarence Wheeler. So [it’s important] to acknowledge the three of us tasked with this work.”
